en: The Therāpadāna: Kaccāyanavagga 6. The Apadāna of the Elder Bāhiya [Verse 1] In the past, when the lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Buddha Kassapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One. [Verse 2] I was a householder at that time, wealthy and possessing great riches; I was a donor who gave alms to the Sangha of monks led by the Buddha. [Verse 3] I saw the Elder Bāhiya, who was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and I offered him a pair of garments as a gift. [Verse 4] Having made that offering, I took refuge in the Triple Gem; having performed that meritorious deed, I passed away from that human existence. [Verse 5] For twenty thousand eons I dwelt in the heavenly realms; through the power of that root of merit, I attained the fruit of Stream-entry. [Verse 6] Now, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, I have realized the state of an Arhat; I have severed all fetters and am free from all bonds. [Verse 7] This is my final birth; there shall be no further existence for me; having reached the goal, I dwell in peace, having attained Nibbāna. [Verse 8] Thus did the Elder Bāhiya speak these verses, which were well-spoken and meaningful;

he who had fulfilled his training and accomplished his task praised the Buddha. [Verse 9] The Buddha, the Teacher, knowing his mind, spoke these words: "Bāhiya, you have indeed done well; you have attained the goal of your training. [Verse 10] "O Bāhiya, this is your final birth; there shall be no further existence for you; having reached the goal, you dwell in peace, having attained Nibbāna. [Verse 11] When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Elder Bāhiya paid homage to the Teacher and, with a heart full of joy, departed from the presence of the Blessed One. [Verse 12] Then, while walking along the path, he was struck by a cow; having reached the end of his life, he attained Parinibbāna right there. [Verse 13] Just as a lamp is extinguished when its oil is exhausted, so too, having abandoned the aggregates, he attained Parinibbāna. [Verse 14] The gods and men who were present there, seeing the Elder Bāhiya pass away, paid him homage with palms joined in reverence. [Verse 15] "This is the final passing of one who has crossed over the flood; he has reached the further shore and stands firm upon the dry land. [Verse 16] Thus did the Elder Bāhiya, having attained Parinibbāna, speak these verses; he who had fulfilled his training and accomplished his task praised the Buddha. “In this hundred-thousandth aeon, the Leader appeared;
He was of great radiance, the foremost in the three worlds.”
By name Padumuttara,
while the Sage was proclaiming the virtues of a bhikkhu of swift direct knowledge.
Having heard this with an uplifted heart,
I performed service for the Great Sage and gave a seven-day offering.
I then paid homage to the Fully Awakened One, the Sage with his disciples,
and aspired to that very state.
Then the Buddha declared of me:
"Behold this brahmin fallen at my feet."
The review of conduct.
With limbs adorned by golden ornaments,
and with skin as white as a conch shell.
With lips like the bimba fruit,
with teeth as white and sharp as jasmine,
and possessing great strength and many virtues—
With the hair on his body standing on end,
he had become a reservoir for a flood of virtues,
his face blossoming with joy.
This is the ground upon which a bhikkhu of swift direct knowledge aspires:
that in the future he will become a Great Hero.
He shall be named Gotama.
He will be his heir to the Dhammas,
a true-born son fashioned by the Dhamma.
‘One named Bāhiya shall become a disciple of the Teacher. Then,
having risen up in joy, he—
For as long as life lasted, O Great Sage,
having performed service, he passed away from here to heaven,
just as one goes to his own abode.
Whether become a god or a human,
one is happy through that karma;
having wandered through the cycle of existence by its force, [one eventually attains liberation].
I experienced prosperity.
Again, when the teaching of the heroic Kassapa was coming to its end, I—
Having ascended the mountain peak and applied himself to the teaching of the Conqueror,
he was pure in virtue and possessed of wisdom.
A builder of the Victor’s dispensation;
then, passing away from there, the five people went to the world of the gods.
Then I was born as Bāhiya in Bhārukaccha,
the most excellent city;
from there, I set out upon a ship.
The ocean was difficult to cross.
Then, after traveling for several days, the ship was wrecked.
Then, having fallen into that terrible and fearsome abode of sea-monsters,
I exerted myself.
Having crossed the great ocean,
he arrived at the excellent port of Suppāra, fainting from exhaustion.
Having clothed myself in a tattered bark garment,
I entered the village for alms;
then that people were delighted.
‘An Arahant has come here.
[Honor him] with food and drink,
with clothing and bedding;’
"And by honoring him with medicine,
we shall become happy. Thus,
at that time, he was a recipient of the requisites.
Honored and worshipped by them,
I gave rise to the improper thought, "I am an arahant."
Then, knowing my mind,
a former deity urged me:
"You do not know the path of means."
"How could you possibly be an arahant?
Being thus reproved by her, I was moved with spiritual urgency and then questioned her.
‘Who are these, and where in the world,
are the Arahants, the supreme among men?
‘The Victor is in Sāvatthī, the abode of the Kosalans.’
Possessing abundant wisdom and excellent, vast intelligence—
this son of the Sakyas, an arahant free from taints,
teaches the Dhamma for the attainment of arahantship.
Having heard those words, he was thrilled,
like a pauper who has found a treasure;
amazed and with a joyful heart, [he attained] supreme arahantship.
To behold Sudassana, whose range is infinite.
Then, having departed from there, [he thought]:
"I shall always see the Teacher, the Victor with the stainless face."
Having entered the delightful forest called Vijita,
I asked the birds, "Where is the Delighter of the World?
Then those honored by men and gods replied:
He has entered the city seeking food;
like a deer eager for the sight of a hunter,
go quickly and pay homage to that Supreme Person.
Then, having gone quickly to Sāvatthī, the supreme city,
I saw him wandering there.
He came here for the sake of alms,
with bowl in hand, free from greed,
making yellow rice appear as he cooked it.
Having approached him,
who resembles the abode of Śrī and whose face bears the splendor of the sun, I bowed down and spoke.
I spoke these words:
“O Gotama, be a refuge for me who have gone astray upon a wrong path.”
‘I am wandering for alms for the sake of ferrying living beings across;
this is not the time for you to give a Dhamma talk.’
Thus spoke the Best of Sages.
Then, longing for the Dhamma, I entreated the Buddha again and again.
He who taught me the Dhamma,
the profound state of emptiness—
having heard his Dhamma, I...
I attained the destruction of the taints;
my life-span being fully exhausted,
oh, how compassionate the Teacher is!
The defilements have been incinerated by me; ... [as before] ...
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me...
[and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth]...
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus did the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya answer,
even though he had fallen upon a heap of refuse.
To a cow possessed by a spirit,
the Greatly Wise One recounted his own former conduct.
That elder attained final nibbāna in Sāvatthī, the most excellent city,
as he was departing from the town.
Having seen Bāhiya, the wise one who wore bark garments and had cast off the scriptures, the Seventh Sage approached him.
The tooth fallen upon the ground,
like the banner of Indra brought low;
its life gone, its defilements withered—
The one who establishes the Victor’s teaching.
Then the Teacher addressed his disciples who delight in the dispensation:
“Take the body of my fellow-celibate, lead it away, and cremate it;
build a stupa and pay it honor.”
He has attained Nibbāna, O Great-Minded One;
he is the foremost of those with swift direct knowledge,
my disciple who carries out my word.
Even a thousand verses composed of meaningless words are not worth a single verse-line that is meaningful.
Having heard which, one attains peace:
where water and earth,
fire and air find no footing.
There the stars do not shine,
nor does the sun illuminate;
there the moon does not gleam.
Darkness does not exist there when a brahmin,
through the sage’s wisdom, knows by himself.
"Then, from both form and the formless,
and from pleasure and pain, one is liberated"—
thus indeed did the Protector speak.
“The Sage, refuge of the three worlds.
Thus indeed did the venerable elder Bāhiya speak these verses.
This is the sixth legend of the elder Bāhiya.
